smt-2022-geometry-01.title: Area with the sine formula
smt-2022-geometry-01.body:
Let $\theta=\angle AEB$; then $\angle CED=\theta$ and $\angle AED=\angle BEC=180^\circ-\theta$, all with the same sine. So $[ABE][CDE]=\frac14\sin^2\theta\cdot AE\cdot BE\cdot CE\cdot DE$ and $[ADE][BCE]=\frac14\sin^2\theta\cdot AE\cdot DE\cdot BE\cdot CE$, which are equal. The answer is $36$.

**Answer: 36**

smt-2022-geometry-02.title: Angle chase
smt-2022-geometry-02.body:
In right triangle formed by the altitude from $B$, $\angle ABH=90^\circ-\angle A$, so $\angle A=70^\circ$. The orthocenter satisfies $\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A=110^\circ$.

$D$ lies on the circle $BHC$ and on the same side of $BC$ as $H$ (it is on ray $CA$), so the inscribed angles $\angle BDC$ and $\angle BHC$ subtend the same chord $BC$ from the same side and are equal: $\angle BDC=110^\circ$. (A coordinate computation for two different triangles gives $110^\circ$ as well.)

**Answer: $110^\circ$**

smt-2022-geometry-03.title: Nine-point circle
smt-2022-geometry-03.body:
The circumcircle of $DEF$ is the nine-point circle of $ABC$. It meets $AD$ again (besides $D$) at the midpoint of $AH$, where $H$ is the orthocenter; likewise $J$ and $K$ are the midpoints of $BH$ and $CH$.

So $\triangle IJK$ is the image of $\triangle ABC$ under the homothety at $H$ with ratio $\frac12$, and $[IJK]=\frac14[ABC]$. The $13$-$14$-$15$ triangle has area $84$ (Heron: $\sqrt{21\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6}=84$), so $[IJK]=21$.

**Answer: 21**

smt-2022-geometry-04.title: Express the side in terms of $b/c$
smt-2022-geometry-04.body:
Let $a=BC=15$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$ and let the square have side $x$. Similarity $\triangle ZBW\sim\triangle ABC$ (with $Z\leftrightarrow A$, $W\leftrightarrow C$) gives $\frac{BZ}{c}=\frac{ZW}{b}=\frac xb$, so $BZ=\frac{xc}b$ and $\angle BZW=\angle A=67.5^\circ$.

The diagonal $ZX$ makes $45^\circ$ with $ZW$, so $\angle XZC=180^\circ-67.5^\circ-45^\circ=67.5^\circ=\angle A$. Hence $\triangle ZXC\sim\triangle ABC$ ($Z\leftrightarrow A$, $X\leftrightarrow B$, $C\leftrightarrow C$), and with $ZX=x\sqrt2$ corresponding to $AB=c$ we get $ZC=\frac{x\sqrt2\,b}{c}$.

Then $a=BZ+ZC=x\left(\frac cb+\frac{\sqrt2\,b}c\right)$, so $x=\dfrac{15}{\frac cb+\frac{\sqrt2\,b}{c}}$. By AM-GM, $\frac cb+\frac{\sqrt2\,b}c\ge2\sqrt[4]2$, with equality for $\frac cb=\sqrt[4]2$ (a valid triangle). So $x\le\frac{15}{2\sqrt[4]2}$ and the maximum area is $x^2=\frac{225}{4\sqrt2}=\frac{225\sqrt2}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{225\sqrt2}{8}$**

smt-2022-geometry-06.title: Tangent lengths
smt-2022-geometry-06.body:
Let $s$ be the semiperimeter. Triangles $BPC$ and $ABC$ share the vertex $B$ and bases $PC$ and $AC$ on the same line, so $\frac{[BPC]}{[ABC]}=\frac{CP}{CA}=\frac{s-c}{b}$ (tangent length from $C$ is $s-c$). Similarly $\frac{[BMC]}{[ABC]}=\frac{BM}{BA}=\frac{s-b}{c}$.

The product is $\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}=\sin^2\frac A2$ (standard half-angle identity). For $A=30^\circ$: $\sin^215^\circ=\frac{1-\cos30^\circ}2=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}=\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}4$.

**Answer: $\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}4$**

smt-2022-geometry-07.title: The incenter of the orthic triangle
smt-2022-geometry-07.body:
Since $7^2+15^2=274<400=20^2$, the triangle is obtuse at $C$. For an obtuse triangle the incenter of the orthic triangle $DEF$ is the obtuse vertex $C$ (angle chase: $AE$ bisects $\angle DEF$ and $BD$ bisects $\angle EDF$, and these lines meet at $C$).

So we need $CH$ where $H$ is the orthocenter. The general formula is $CH=2R|\cos C|$. Here $\cos C=\frac{7^2+15^2-20^2}{2\cdot7\cdot15}=-\frac{126}{210}=-\frac35$, so $\sin C=\frac45$ and $R=\frac{AB}{2\sin C}=\frac{20}{8/5}=\frac{25}2$. Then $CH=2\cdot\frac{25}2\cdot\frac35=15$. (A coordinate computation confirms $15$.)

**Answer: 15**

smt-2022-geometry-08.title: Homothety at $P$
smt-2022-geometry-08.body:
The homothety $h$ at $P$ taking $\Gamma$ to $\Omega$ sends $X\mapsto A$ and $Y\mapsto B$, hence takes the circle $O_2$ (diameter $XY$) to $O_1$ (diameter $AB$). So $P$ is the external centre of similitude of $O_1,O_2$, and the common tangent $TM$ passes through $P$ with $h(M)=T$. Let $k$ be the ratio.

$F$ lies on $O_2$ ($\angle XFY=90^\circ$), so the power of $P$ with respect to $O_2$ is $PF\cdot PX=12\cdot27=324$, and since $PM$ is tangent to $O_2$, $PM=18$. Then $PT=PM+MT=36$ and $k=\frac{PT}{PM}=2$.

Thus $PA=2PX=54$, $PY=\frac12PB=25$, and the foot $F_1$ of $B$ on $AP$ satisfies $PF_1=2PF=24$, so $AF_1=30$. Also $FY=\sqrt{25^2-12^2}=\sqrt{481}$.

In $\triangle ABP$, $H=AF_2\cap BF_1$ with $F_2$ the foot of $A$ on $PB$. Then $\angle F_1AH=90^\circ-\angle APB=\angle FYP$, so right triangles $AF_1H$ and $YFP$ are similar: $\frac{AF_1}{AH}=\frac{FY}{PY}$, giving $AH=\frac{30\cdot25}{\sqrt{481}}=\frac{750}{\sqrt{481}}$. (A coordinate computation confirms $\approx34.197$.)

**Answer: $\frac{750}{\sqrt{481}}$**

smt-2022-geometry-09.title: Show $\angle A=72^\circ$
smt-2022-geometry-09.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle A$, $\gamma=\angle C$. Mark $T$ on ray $AC$ with $AT=AK$; since $AK=AC+CL+LA$, we get $CT=CL+LA$. Mark $B'$ on ray $LB$ with $LB'=AL$; then $CB'=CL+LB'=CL+LA=CT$. The external bisector $CK$ makes $\angle B'CK=\angle TCK=90^\circ+\frac\gamma2$, so $\triangle KCB'\cong\triangle KCT$ (SAS), hence $\angle CB'K=\angle CTK=\frac\alpha2$ (as $AKT$ is isosceles with apex angle $\alpha$).

Comparing with $\angle CB'A=\angle LAB'$ (as $LA=LB'$) shows that $B'$ can lie neither strictly between $L$ and $B$ (which would force $\angle CB'K<\frac\alpha2$) nor beyond $B$ (which would force $\angle CB'K>\frac\alpha2$). So $B'=B$, i.e. $LB=LA=1$, and $\angle ABC=\angle LAB=\frac\alpha2=36^\circ$, so $\alpha=72^\circ$.

Then $\angle C=180^\circ-72^\circ-36^\circ=72^\circ$, and in $\triangle ALC$: $\angle LAC=36^\circ$, $\angle C=72^\circ$, so $\angle ALC=72^\circ$ and $AC=AL=1$.

Check: with these angles $AL=LB=AC=1$, $AK$ equals the perimeter of $\triangle ACL$ ($\approx2.618$ in a coordinate computation).

**Answer: 1**

smt-2022-geometry-10.title: Radical axis and power of a point
smt-2022-geometry-10.body:
Let $I=HA\cap DC$, $s=\sqrt{60}$, and let $\Gamma_0$ be the circumcircle of the octagon. The circles $(HAK)$ and $\Gamma_0$ share the chord $HA$, and $(DCK)$ and $\Gamma_0$ share the chord $DC$, so $I$ is the radical centre of the three circles. If $(HAK)$ and $(DCK)$ are tangent at $K$, their radical axis is the common tangent at $K$, and it passes through $I$; therefore $IK^2$ equals the power of $I$ with respect to $(HAK)$, which equals its power with respect to $\Gamma_0$, namely $ID\cdot IC$. Conversely every point at that distance from $I$ works. So $\mathcal K$ is the circle centred at $I$ with $r^2=ID\cdot IC$.

Compute $IC$: $\triangle HDI\sim\triangle ACI$ gives $\frac{HD}{AC}=\frac{DI}{CI}=\frac{s+CI}{CI}$. Since $HD=\sqrt2\,AC$ (in the regular octagon, $AE=HD$ and $\triangle ACE$ is an isosceles right triangle), $\sqrt2=1+\frac{s}{CI}$, so $CI=\frac{s}{\sqrt2-1}=s(1+\sqrt2)$ and $DI=CI+s=s(2+\sqrt2)$.

$ID\cdot IC=s^2(1+\sqrt2)(2+\sqrt2)=s^2(4+3\sqrt2)$. The area is $\pi s^2(4+3\sqrt2)=(240+180\sqrt2)\pi$ for $s^2=60$. (A coordinate computation confirms.)

**Answer: $(240+180\sqrt2)\pi$**
